content:
For the English version of this story, please see 

Nunavut Sport and Recreation awards gala honours leaders, volunteers

.







ᓯᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᓂᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᕙᖕᓂᖅ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐅᕙᓂ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐅᕙᓂ ᐊᕐᓴᕐᓃᑦ ᑐᔪᕐᒥᕕᒃᒥ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 3-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑕᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒥᕐᖑᐃᕐᓯᕐᕕᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᑐᙵᓱᒃᑎᑦᑎᔨᐅᖃᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐅᑯᓂᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᖏᓐᓂ.




ᓄᕗᐊᓕᐊ ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᑭᙵᕐᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᑖᖅᑎᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐆᒥᖓ ᑳᒻ ᐃᐅ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓵᓚᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᕙᒃᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᐅᔭᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᔨᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᔭᐅᓕᖅᖢᖢᓂ ᕼᐋᒻᒪᓚᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕌᓂᒃᑳᖓᑕ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ.




“ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐊᓘᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᓲᖃᐃᒻᒪ ᖃᓄᐃᑦᑕᐃᓕᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᕈᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒨᖓᓂᖓᓄᑦ, ᐃᓱᒪᒃᑯᓪᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᒪᓂᕐᓴᐅᔾᔪᑎᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᕐᓴᕈᑎᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐃᓅᓯᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᕈᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᕐᒧᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᕙᐃᔅᐳᒃᑯ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 8-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᐅᓇ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕᒃ 18-ᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᖅ 40-ᖏᓐᓃᑦᑐᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕᖕᓂ 5-ᓂ 12-ᓄ 4:00 ᐅᓪᓗᒃᑯᑦ 6:00 ᑎᑭᓐᓇᓱᖕᓂᖓᓂ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᑉ ᐃᓗᐊᒍᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᒃᑯᕕᒃᒥᑦ.




ᑐᓴᕐᓈᖅᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᑯᐊ ᐃᙱᖅᖢᑎ Black Eyed Peas ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᓯᖏᑦ ᐃᙱᕐᑏᑦ ᑐᓴᕐᓈᕈᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᓂᐱᑭᓵᓯᒪᓪᓗᓂ, ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᑖᒃᑯᓂᖓ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᐅᓪᓗ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖏᑦᑕᓕ ᐊᓯᐊᒎᖓᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕋᓱᒃᖢᓂ.
















ᐃᒡᓘ ᐃᓗᐊᓂ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕋᓱᒃᖢᓂ ᐃᓱᒫᓘᑎᖃᕋᓂ “ᐃᓐᓇᕐᓄᑦ ᐱᒡᒍᓴᐅᑎᐅᓇᔭᙳᐊᖅᑐᓂᒃ.”




“ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᓲᕐᓗ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒦᖅᑰᔨᓐᓇᕈᓐᓃᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓱᕈᓰᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕐᓂᕐᓴᐅᓕᖃᑦᑕᕐᒪᑕ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᐅᑯᐊ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐅᕋᓱᒐᑎᒃ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᑦ ᖁᕕᐊᓲᑎᖃᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᑦ ᑭᙵᐃᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓪᓗᑎᒃ.




“ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔨᐅᕙᒃᑐᑦ ᐆᒻᒪᑎᒋᔭᐅᒻᒪᕆᒃᑐᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖏᓐᓂᒃ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨᖓ ᐃᐅᕋᓐ ᕌᐱᓐᓴᓐ ᐅᖄᓚᐅᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 8-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.

title: News quiz Oct. 17 | Videography and Valentine’s Day volunteers
content:
A news quiz? Why not. Let’s get into it!




1.

 Nunavut Premier John Main spoke to Nunatsiaq News last week to give an update on the GN’s stalled elder van project. What did he say?




A.

 “The vans are ready to rock and roll.”




B.

 “We’ve got the vans, we just need drivers.”




C.

 “The update is, as of right now, they’re still not operating.”




2.

 Kinngait’s youth group won a volunteer award on Oct. 3. It has run a number of events, including a breakfast on what holiday?




A.

 Valentine’s Day




B.

 Christmas




C.

 Nunavut Day




3.

 Sonia Caron, Quebec’s new representative for the Ungava Riding, is a member of Parti Québécois, which has promised to revisit a referendum on Quebec separatism. What did she say to Nunatsiaq News about what that might mean for the province’s Inuit?




A.

 She said she would ask her constituents what they think.




B.

 She declined to comment.




C.

 She said she would defer to the premier on the issue.
















4.

A.

 Oct. 20




B.

 Oct. 26




C.

 Oct. 31




5.

 A person in Gjoa Haven was assaulted earlier this month while doing what?




A.

 Canvassing for Statistics Canada.




B.

 Driving a water truck.

title: The world is ending, and I feel fine
content:
A friend told me a story this summer about

 a smokey day in Minnesota, where she lives. When she complained about the haze to her 13-year-old nephew, he responded: “That’s just summer.”




It wasn’t long ago that wildfire smoke was a characteristic of summer mostly limited to western North America, where conditions are drier.




But, in just a few years, that has drastically changed. Evidence of climate change is everywhere: it’s in the sea ice of the North — much less predictable now — and unbreathable air across the south. (And 

parts

 of the North.)




When we think about and imagine the collapse of civilization, the conversation usually revolves around the world becoming uninhabitable due to climate change.

wrote about

A change like that could bring Iqaluit’s mean daily temperature in January from -26 C to -16 C. 




For comparison, Iqaluit’s average daily temperature 

increased

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: RCMP charge former Kugaaruk hamlet employee with fraud
content:
A former Hamlet of Kugaaruk employee is facing six counts of fraud-related charges, after a year-long RCMP investigation.




Police have charged 29-year-old Hanah Arafiles with fraud over $5,000, forgery, uttering forged documents, drawing document without authority, theft under $5,000 and possession of property obtained by crime.




Sgt. George Henrie announced the charges in a news release on Friday.




In August 2025, police opened an investigation after the hamlet alleged that a former employee had defrauded it earlier that year.




One year later, a Nunavut judge issued an arrest warrant.




On Oct. 8, the Ontario Provincial Police arrested Arafiles in Pembroke, Ont.




She has been released from custody and is scheduled to appear in Iqaluit court on Nov. 2.

title: New Nunavik rehabilitation service to begin with 46 patients
content:

title: Judge puts Mary River Mine’s future in hands of neutral decision-makers
content:
Final say over the future of the Mary River iron mine is in the hands of two neutral, court-appointed parties, an Ontario judge has ordered.




Justice Jana Steele’s decision on Oct. 14 comes as Baffinland Iron Mines Corp. 

enters

 a sale and investment solicitation process, an effort to keep the mine operational after the company 

announced

 in May that it 

could not repay

 roughly $1.2 billion to various lenders.




The mine contributes roughly 25 per cent of Nunavut’s gross domestic product.




“At this time, the alternative to a transaction is a liquidation, which would have a devastating impact … including the loss of over 1,200 jobs,” said Steele, a superior court judge.




Export Development Canada and the company’s other lenders proposed that a court appointed monitor and neutral chief restructuring officer should have final say over any potential deal. Baffinland wanted a committee of shareholder representatives in that role.




“While the distinction may appear academic at first blush, the ultimate decision-maker in the [sale process] will have the authority to make critical decisions, including waiving bidding criteria, selecting the successful bid, and finalizing any resulting transaction,” Steele said in her decision, before concluding an independent decision-maker is the “best path forward” for the company.

author: Randi Beers
title: Feeding our family — and the community
content:
Dear Nunatsiaq News,




I am writing to share a story about my father Walter J. Porter of Gjoa Haven, Nunavut, and a tradition of sharing that I have witnessed since I was a girl.




My father is blind, but he remains connected to our Inuit traditions and our community through sharing country food. His son provides him with caribou meat, while other family members help butcher it.




What makes this tradition special is that the meat is for our family, as well as for anybody else. It is placed outside so that community members can take whatever they want. People are welcome to take some home for themselves and their families.




My father is happy to be outside for a while when people gather to collect the meat. There is company outside, and people come and go as they take what they need. It is a simple but meaningful way of bringing people together through sharing.




As far back as I can remember, this has been part of my life. I was little when I first noticed this tradition. My father’s grandchildren now see what sharing means.

author: Daron Letts
title: Esthetician prepares for New York Fashion Week
content:
Odette Wills wasn’t allowed to wear makeup as a teenager.




Now, the 26-year-old Iqaluit esthetician is preparing to work as a makeup artist backstage at New York Fashion Week, from Feb. 12 to 14.




“I still think I have a long way to go,” Wills said during an interview in her new home-based Authentic Glow Studio which opened in May, the product of a New Year’s resolution.




Wills travelled to New York City for a week in September, where she completed a course at Aimakeup Beauty Academy in Westside Manhattan’s Chelsea neighbourhood and 

befriended Instagram influencer Ipek.




“Odette is very talented,” said Aiyma, the school’s founder who goes by one name, in a phone interview Tuesday.




New York Fashion Week, held in February and September every year, features fashion industry shows throughout Manhattan and marks the debut of many international labels.




In the fall, Aiyma’s students (not including Wills) provided makeup for models working with brand labels such as Geo in Style, F&W and Amari Carter, among others. 

In December, Wills will learn what brands she will be working with, Aiyma said.

She has added exfoliating, cleansing, and non-medical facial massage to her studio’s services.

title: Taloyoak’s new Pangniq High School unveiled with public ceremony
content:
Metalshop students at Taloyoak’s new $90-million Pangniq High School crafted the qulliq that will be lit at an unveiling ceremony set for Friday. 




The school overlooks the community from atop a raised plot of ground next to the airport.




Its stature in the landscape is mirrored by its name —  pangniq, an Inuktitut term for the most prominent bull in a caribou herd. Students helped choose that name as part of a contest last year.




“The school is outstanding — state of the art,” said first-year principal Rodney Drover Wednesday in a phone interview.




The school’s 16 staff members and 200 students from grades 7 to 12 began their fall semester in the 3,300-square-metre facility for the first time since

It’s the fifth school completed by Iqaluit-based general contractor Pilitak Enterprises Ltd., Winnipeg-based Accutech Engineering Inc., and Parkin Architects, which has offices in Ontario and B.C.

title: Proposed federal lands act amendment could complicate devolution: premier
content:
Ottawa’s tinkering with its Territorial Lands Act could throw a wrench in Nunavut’s devolution work, says Premier John Main.




He was speaking to a 

Senate Standing Committee on Indigenous Peoples Oct. 6 during a hearing about mineral rights in the territory.




Nunavut is preparing the legislative framework that will allow the territorial government to take control of a vast majority of its Crown land. To do so, it’s mirroring several federal acts, including the Territorial Lands Act, to finalize devolution, which is set to happen April 1, 2027.




The act governs use of Crown land in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut, including its sale or lease,

 

mining rights and environmental regulations.




But the Territorial Lands Act could change as its being mirrored.




Working its way through Senate hearings is Bill C-31, which proposes amendments the act that would 

allow Canada’s federal cabinet, on the recommendation of the northern affairs minister, to cancel or restrict mineral rights on Crown land in Nunavut if it determines doing so is in the national interest.




“The timing of Bill C-31 creates a particular challenge,” said Main in his opening remarks to the committee.

author: David Venn
title: President, community director roles up for grabs in QIA election
content:
The Qikiqtani Inuit Association is looking for its next president.




It’s also looking for community directors in Iqaluit, Igloolik, Kimmirut, Sanirajak, Clyde River, Pond Inlet and Sanikiluaq, said a news release issued Thursday by Markoosie Qaunirq, spokesperson for QIA.




Each position carries a four-year term.




The nomination period for the election runs from Nov. 9 to 13.




Eligible voters must be Inuit, enrolled under the Nunavut Agreement; at least 16 years old; and have resided in the Qikiqtani Region for one year or more, according to the release.




The current QIA president Olayuk Akesuk 

won

 the 2022 election over Paul Okalik, with 61.2 per cent of the vote. He had served in the role since the fall of 2021, when he took over from P.J. Akeeagok, who resigned to run for MLA.




Election day is set for Dec. 14.

title: Nunavik health board developing local rehabilitation services
content:
Nunavik residents could have greater access to specialized rehabilitation services closer to home through a new partnership aimed at providing orthotics, prosthetics and positioning services within the region.




The Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services announced the partnership Oct. 13 in a news release with Quebec Health Centre-West-of-Montreal University and the Constance-Lethbridge Rehabilitation Centre.




With the initiative, residents will have access to equipment fitting and follow-up care without needing to travel outside the region for some services.




Orthotics are devices, such as braces or specially fitted supports, that help stabilize or protect parts of the body. Prosthetics are artificial limbs or other devices that replace a missing body part. Positioning services involve selecting and adapting equipment, such as wheelchairs, seating systems and other supports.




A technologist specializing in orthotics, prosthetics and orthopedic care will be regularly present in Nunavik, the release said.




Assessments and moulding will be conducted in local communities, allowing patients to receive some services without travelling south.




When devices must be manufactured in Montreal, they will be transported back to Nunavik for fitting and delivery to patients.

author: Daron Letts
title: Carpentry to return to Victor Sammurtok School
content:
Woodworking will soon be back on the curriculum at Chesterfield Inlet’s Victor Sammurtok School following a three-year absence.




“There is so much value in a woodshop,” said principal Jacques Theriault during an interview earlier this semester. “With woodworking, we’re introducing a trade and there’s a lifetime career right there.”




The new woodshop is expected to be in operation in time to offer the program to students by mid-January, he added.




The school had a functioning woodshop in the past, but former staff converted the space into a weight room following the COVID-19 pandemic.




The room is still equipped with industrial ventilation and wiring to accommodate the electrical demands of a fully functioning shop.




When 

Theriault became principal in January 2025, he immediately began searching for funders to reinstate the woodshop, though he admired the quality of the weight room, he said.




It boasts a state-of-the-art rowing machine that connects to other rowers online and other high-end exercise equipment. The exercise space will move into a smaller room across the hall, Theriault said.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Man dies after altercation in Iqaluit
content:
RCMP are treating the death of a man involved in an altercation in Iqaluit last week as a homicide.




Police responded to calls about an altercation at around 9:55 p.m. on Oct. 6, according to a press release issued Wednesday by Sgt. George Henrie.




Two people were transported to the Qikiqtani General Hospital with life-threatening injuries.




“Despite life saving measures, one male succumbed to his injuries,” Henrie wrote.




RCMP identified the man who died as 38-year-old Robert Kipanik.




The other person, who has yet to be identified, was medivaced to Ottawa, where he is in stable condition.




The RCMP’s Major Crime Unit is investigating.

Last week, the Qikiqtani Inuit Association announced $15 million for the Saviruut Building, which will house hamlet wellness initiatives and a federally funded early childhood development program.




“It’s good to see that we’re getting more infrastructure, because the need is there,” senior administrative officer John Ivey said in an interview with Nunatsiaq News.




The hamlet asked QIA to fund a wellness centre a few years before Ivey joined its administration.




The regional organization, responsible for just over 51 per cent of Nunavut’s Inuit population, allocated the money from its Indigenous Community Infrastructure Fund.




QIA selected Arctic Fresh Projects Inc. as the contractor and expects materials to ship to the hamlet next year, said a news release issued last week by the Inuit organization.




Once built, the facility will support “initiatives that promote healing and the transfer of Inuit traditional knowledge and worldview to future generations,” said QIA spokesperson Markoosie Qaunirq.
















It will also be home to the Aboriginal Head Start early childhood program, to which the Public Health Agency of Canada provided $3.2 million.




Ivey said he’s unsure when Arctic Fresh plans to complete the building.

title: Iqaluit crosswalk lights temporarily shut down
content:
Iqaluit’s only controlled 

crosswalk

The lighted crossing is adjacent to the intersection of Niaqungusiariaq Road and Queen Elizabeth Way.

author: Daron Letts
title: Nominations for KIA elections to open Oct. 26
content:
Nominations for five seats on the Kivalliq Inuit Association board of directors will open on Oct. 26.




The election is scheduled for Dec. 14, c

hief returning officer Penny Taylor announced Tuesday, in the association’s notice of election.




The roles include vice-president and secretary/treasurer, as well as the community director positions in Naujaat, Rankin Inlet and Whale Cove.




“This year’s election is more than a procedural milestone — it is an opportunity for Inuit across the Kivalliq region to help shape the future of their communities and strengthen Inuit-led governance,” Taylor said in an email on Tuesday. “

The voices of Inuit voters and nominees are essential to that work.”




The nomination period closes at 3 p.m. on Nov. 9.




Advance polls will be held on Dec. 7, Taylor said.




Mobile polls will also visit schools, elders’ centres, health centres, mine sites, boarding homes, healing facilities, and Winnipeg’s Uquutaq Medical Boarding Home. Schedules for each community will be posted by Nov. 30.
















Eligible voters must be an Inuk enrolled under the Nunavut Agreement aged 16 years or older as of Dec. 14, 2026, and regularly reside in the Kivalliq region.




KIA is the designated Inuit organization under the Nunavut Final Agreement and one of three regional Inuit organizations associated with Nunavut Tunngavik Inc.

content:
Police have charged a Chesterfield Inlet youth with first-degree murder following the death of a man in the hamlet early Friday morning.




Nunavut RCMP issued a news release about the incident Tuesday.




Officers arrived on scene at 1 a.m. following a report of gunfire and located a man “with injuries consistent with a gunshot wound,” the release said.




The victim was transported to the local health centre, where he was pronounced dead.




Police arrested a youth and the Nunavut RCMP Major Crime Unit laid charges that same day.




The youth, whose identity is protected by law, is in custody and scheduled to appear in court in Iqaluit on Nov. 16.




It’s unclear what, if any, relation there is between the accused and victim.
















RCMP are not providing any further details, the release said.

ᓅᑕᐅᓂᖓ, ᑭᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᔭᕆᑐᔪᓄᑦ ᐊᑲᐅᙱᓕᐅᕈᑕᐅᔪᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᕐᔪᐊᒥ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᑲᑐᔾᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐊᖑᔪᒥ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 30−ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᑎᓕᐅᖅᑕᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᓕᐊᕆ ᐅᐊᑦᒧᑦ, ᐅᖓᕙ ᑐᓚᑦᑕᕕᒃ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᕕᖓᓂ ᐃᓱᒻᒥᖅᑐᐃᔨᖓᓂ; ᐊᒻᒪᔭᓇᕗ ᒥᐅᓂᒃ−ᐅᐊᑦᑭᓐᔅ, ᓄᓇᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᕕᒃᑐᖅᓯᒪᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᔪᓂ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᕐᓇᙱᑦᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓄᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐃᓱᒻᒥᖅᑐᐃᔨᖓᓐᓂ.




“ᓅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᓯᒪᕗᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑲᔪᓯᓂᐊᖅᐳᑦ ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᑕᒪᒃᑭᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᐊᑦᑕᓇᙱᑦᑐᒥ ᓅᑕᐅᕌᓂᒃᐸᑕ,” ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᖅ ᐅᖃᖅᓯᒪᕗᖅ.




ᓅᑕᐅᓂᖓ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᕗᖅ ᐱᖓᓱᐃᓕᖓᔪᒥ ᐊᖏᕈᑕᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᓚᖃᕐᒥᔪᒥᒃ Argyle Inc.−ᑯᑦ ᐊᑯᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐸᖅᑭᕝᕕᐅᔪᒥ, ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᕐᓄᑦ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᐅᔪᒥ ᒪᓐᑐᕆᐋᓪ ᓯᓚᑎᑦᑎᐊᖓᓂ ᐳᐊᐃᓐᑦ ᑭᓕᐊᕐᒥ.




“ᐊᖏᕈᑎ ᑐᕌᕋᓱᐊᖅᐳᖅ ᑐᓂᓯᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᑦᑕᓇᙱᑦᑐᒥ, ᐸᖅᑭᑦᑎᐊᖅᑐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᒧᑦ ᐊᒃᑐᐃᓂᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐆᒪᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᕙᑎᐅᔪᒥ, ᐃᓚᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐃᓛᓐᓂᓚᐅᓱᖓᕐᒥ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᖅᑯᓯᑐᖃᖅᑎᒍᑦ ᓂᕿᓂᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᖓᓱᓂ ᐃᓄᖕᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᐅᔪᓂ,” ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐊᖑᔪᖅ ᑲᔪᓯᕗᖅ.




ᑕᒪᒃᑭᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᓅᑕᐅᒍᑎᒃ, ᑐᓵᔨᐊᐱᒃ ᒪᑐᓂᐊᖅᐳᖅ.
















ᐅᐊᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒥᐅᓂᒃ-ᐅᐊᑦᑭᓐᔅ ᑕᒪᒃᑭᑦ ᐊᐅᓪᓚᖅᓯᒪᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 1−ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐅᕈᓐᓇᙱᖦᖢᑎᒃ, ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᖓᑕ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᓂ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ.




ᑰᔾᔪᐊᕐᒥ, ᓯᕗᓪᓕᐅᔪᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᕙᓪᓕᐊᕗᖅ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᔪᓐᓇᕋᔭᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᖏᓂᖓᓂ ᑎᑭᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᑐᓵᔨᐊᐱᖕᒥ ᒫᓐᓇᐅᔪᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᒐᒃᓴᐃᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᖓᓐᓄᑦ, ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᖅ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ. ᐊᑭᖓᓂ ᓇᓚᐅᑦᑖᕆᔭᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᓂᕆᐅᒋᔭᐅᕗᖅ ᖃᖓᒃᑲᓐᓂᖅ ᑕᒪᑐᒪᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᖑᔪᒥ.




ᑐᓵᔨᐊᐱᒃ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ “ᐱᔭᕆᑐᔪᓂ” ᐊᑲᐅᙱᓕᐅᕈᑕᐅᔪᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᕐᔪᐊᑉ ᐅᖅᑰᓴᐅᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᐅᔪᒥ, ᐱᑎᑦᑎᔪᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨᐅᔪᓂ ᕿᓂᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓅᑕᐅᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓂᕆᐅᒐᒃᓴᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᐃᑉᕆᓕᒥ 13−ᓄᑦ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᕐᓄᑦ, 10−ᖑᔪᑦ

That same day Capt. George Tyson encountered a party of Inuit travelling by boat in the sound, off on a caribou hunting trip. 




From them he learned that the other Inuit who had promised to accompany him had changed their minds and already gone inland hunting caribou. He prevailed on some of the newcomers to join his venture, but they declined. 




Three days later, Tyson put in at the American whaling station at Kekerten to pick up skins. 




He noted, “We were employed today preparing a place in the vessel’s hold for the Esquimaux to live during the passage to Greenland.” 




There he took one more man, three women and two children. Was one of these women a wife for Alokee? 




With these additions, the complement of Inuit was 15, five each of men, women and children.

There were also 30 dogs and a number of sleds aboard.

title: Supreme Court delivers landmark decision on Indigenous offenders and victims
content:
A Supreme Court of Canada decision on Friday has clarified the factors that judges should account for when a defendant and victim are both Indigenous.




The landmark case, 

R. v. Cope

, concerns Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaw man from Nova Scotia who pleaded guilty to assaulting his partner, a Mi’kmaw woman, in 2021.




The Supreme Court weighed in on a trial judge’s decision to sentence Cope to five years in prison and the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal’s decision to reduce that sentence to three years.




On Friday, the Supreme Court upheld the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal’s ruling, which accounted for Cope’s mental illness and substance use.




“The sentencing judge should have linked the mental health factor to the offender’s moral blameworthiness on the aggravated assault offence, but failed to do so,” wrote Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin, writing for the majority of the judges. “The court of appeal was therefore correct to intervene and it arrived at a just and appropriate sentence.”




Four of nine judges sided with the Nova Scotia provincial court’s original ruling, which dismissed recommendations from community members who proposed no further jail time and opted for a treatment program instead.

The project stalled in 2025, at the end of the previous government’s term, due to a lack of an operating budget.

ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᐊᕐᕕᐊᓂᒃ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᖅ ᐅᕘᓇ ᓴᒃᑯ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕈᑎᓄᑦ, ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑯᐸᐃᒃᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᖅᑎᓄᑦ (ᐊᔾᔨᙳᐊᖅ ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᑕᓃᔅ ᑯᓱᒐᖅ/ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᑯᐊᐳᕇᓴᓐᑯᓐᓂᑦ)




ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖃᕐᑐᖅ 15-ᓂ, 14 ᐃᓅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑭᐅᕈᓕᓐ ᓅᑦ, ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖅ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕈᑎᒃᑯᑦ, ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑯᐸᒃᒥᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᖅᑎᓄᑦ RG Solution-ᑯᓐᓄᑦ, ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃᒥ. ᑖᒃᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᖁᓕᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᖅᐸᒃᑐᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᓂᒃᑰᖓᙱᖢᑎᒃ.




“ᐊᑕᐅᓯᑐᐊᕐᒥ ᐃᓅᙱᑦᑐᒥ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖃᕐᑐᑦ, ᐅᕙᓐᓂ,” ᓅᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




2028 ᐊᕐᕌᒍ ᑎᑭᑉᐸᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑐᑦ 40-ᐅᓕᕐᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐃᓚᖃᕐᓗᑎᒃ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᖃᓪᓚᕆᒃᐸᒃᑐᓂᑦ, ᕿᔪᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ, ᓱᓪᓗᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᐊᔭᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ, ᒋᐸᓐᔅ ᐅᖃᕐᒥᔪᖅ.
















ᐱᔪᓐᓇᐅᑎᖃᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᖅ ᒪᑯᓂᖓ ᕿᔪᓕᕆᔨᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᓪᓚᕆᒃᑐᓂᒃ ᐅᓇ ᑲᒻᐸᓂᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᖅᓴᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᕐᓗᑎᒃ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᓯᓚᑦᑐᖅᓴᕐᕕᒃᒥ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᒃᑯᑎᑖᖅᑎᑕᐅᓇᓱᒡᓗᑎᒃ ᓴᓇᔨᐅᔪᑦ, ᓅᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᓴᒃᑯᑯᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᔪᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᒃᓴᓂ ᑕᒪᐅᖔᕐᓯᒪᙱᑦᑐᓂ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓂᐊᕋᓱᒋᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᒪᐅᓇ ᐃᖏᕐᕋᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ, ᐋᖄᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᐊᓂᒃᑕᐅᑎᑦᑎᔾᔪᑎᒃᑯᑦ.




ᒫᓂ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᖅ ᐱᖓᓲᓕᖓᓪᓗᒍ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃ, ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᓴᓇᔭᐅᓕᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ 2023-ᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᔾᔪᑎ

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Videographer assaulted while filming for Gjoa Haven clean energy initiative
content:
A videographer 

was assaulted Monday in Gjoa Haven while filming for an energy-saving initiative, says Mayor Raymond Quqshuun Sr.




“The hamlet is taking the incident seriously while respecting the privacy of those involved,” Quqshuun said in an email to Nunatsiaq News on Thursday.




It’s unclear what exactly happened but the victim was uninjured, Quqshuun said. The incident was reported to the hamlet but not the RCMP.




The mayor did not say if the victim was visiting the community and declined to provide any further details.




In a Facebook post on Wednesday, the account for the hamlet’s mayor described the victim as a videographer involved in Gjoa Haven’s Winter Clean Energy Challenge, an initiative that encourages households to reduce energy use in the winter.




“Incidents like these are unusual,” Quqshuun said in his email, adding that the community is known to be “particularly warm and welcoming” to guests.




Run by the Kikitak Housing Association, Qulliq Energy Corp., the hamlet maintenance team and Yukon University’s Northern Energy Innovation program, the challenge provides participants with weather-stripping material, window film and energy-friendly shower heads.
















The household with the largest energy reduction wins an electric side-by-side utility terrain vehicle, Quqshuun said.

author: Daron Letts
title: Crosswalk crash stalls Iqaluit traffic
content:
A downed crosswalk pole on Niaqungusiariaq Rd., across from Iqaluit’s Qikiqtani General Hospital clinic entrance, slowed traffic for 90 minutes, following a two-car collision at around noon on Thursday.




“Everyone was checked at the scene, and one person went to the hospital on their own afterwards for further assessment,” said city spokesperson Geoff Byrne in an email.




The city warned drivers of the traffic disruption in a public service announcement issued shortly after 12 p.m.




Two RCMP vehicles blocked Niaqungusiariaq Rd. about two hundred metres past the Sailijaaqvik boarding home at the southeast corner of the intersection. An RCMP truck also blocked Queen Elizabeth Way about 100 metres from the entrance to Astro Hill.




Traffic was backed up on Niaqungusiariaq Road all the way up to Joamie School for approximately 90 minutes while city workers removed the pole, broken in two places, with heavy equipment. The crew also filled-in the hole left behind.




The intersection is the site of Iqaluit’s first controlled 

crosswalk

, which was installed in fall 2024.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: RCMP arrest suspect in Pangnirtung shooting
content:
The RCMP has arrested a 21-year-old man in relation to a shooting in Pangnirtung on Tuesday afternoon.




Police received reports of gunshots at around 4:03 p.m. Tuesday. Ten minutes later, they arrested Jonah Kuniliusie, according to a news release issued by Sgt. George Henrie on Thursday.




Kuniliusie faces two counts of endangering life, two counts of pointing a firearm, two counts of aggravated assault, and the unlawful possession of a weapon in public. He also faces three counts for breach of probation.




The RCMP was not immediately available to answer questions about the incident.




Deputy mayor Markus Wilcke said the event harmed everyone in the community, either directly or indirectly, including children who were nearby 

when the shooting happened

.




Kuniliusie remains in custody and will have his next court appearance on Oct. 20 in Iqaluit.

author: Daron Letts
title: Nunavut Sport and Recreation awards gala honours leaders, volunteers
content:
Leadership and volunteerism were recognized during the Nunavut Sport and Recreation awards gala at Iqaluit’s Aqsarniit hotel on Saturday.




The Recreation and Parks Association of Nunavut co-hosted the event in partnership with the NU Sport Federation and the territorial government’s sport and recreation division.




Novoalia Carriere of Kinngait earned the Calm Air Youth Leader of the Year award for his work as a summer camp supervisor and now as head of the hamlet’s after-school program.




“Sport is important for young people because it promotes healthy physical growth, builds mental resilience, and teaches essential life and social skills,” said Carriere over Facebook Thursday.




The 18-year-old athlete cares for up to 40 children aged five through 12 from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. weekdays at the youth centre.




With the music of Black Eyed Peas and other pop artists filling the background at low volume, Carriere tries to create an atmosphere that’s distinct from school and home.




He cycles through creative indoor activities to foster social connection without any concern for “competition or adult expectations.”

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Nanuq is king of Arctic-inspired chess set
content:
A men’s group in Cambridge Bay has helped create a Nunavut-inspired chess set that features polar bears, grizzlies, snowy owls, rabbits and muskoxen.




Clifford Nzombato plays an Arctic-inspired Snakes and Ladders game he helped create at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa. The board features northern wildlife. Players who land on an animal’s mouth slide down to its tail. (Photo by Nehaa Bimal)




Hunter Nathan Kaoslead has led the Cambridge Bay men’s group for two years. He said the idea emerged last year as the men played chess, Snakes and Ladders and cards at their weekly game nights.







“As we were playing, we said to each other, ‘Wouldn’t it be awesome if these were Arctic animal pieces?'” Kaoslead said.




Kaoslead first drew the animals on a napkin, then figured out how they could replace traditional chess pieces. He also consulted elders on names and characteristics.




The resulting Isumaniq Chess includes a polar bear, or nanuq in Inuinnaqtun, as the king; a grizzly bear, or akhak, as the queen; a snowy owl, or okpik, as the bishop; a rabbit, or okalik, as the knight; and a muskox, or umingmak, as the rook.




An inuksuk represents the pawns.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: New Ungava MNA promises to bring Nunavik to the table
content:
Newly elected Ungava MNA Sonia Caron says her first priority after taking office will be to travel north and begin building relationships with Nunavik’s communities.




Caron, a Parti Québécois candidate and longtime educator from Chibougamau, won the northern riding in Monday’s provincial election with 39.5 per cent of the vote. The PQ formed a minority government, winning 59 of 127 seats in Quebec’s national assembly.




“I feel honored and very proud that the people of Ungava have placed their trust in me for the next term,” Caron said in a French interview Wednesday.




Caron succeeds Coalition Avenir Québec member Denis Lamothe, who represented the riding since 2018. He was a member of the Coalition party’s governments led by former premiers François Legault and Christine Fréchette.

Coalition Avenir Québec, which won elections in 2018 and 2022, was wiped out Monday, losing all it seats across the province.




Caron said she plans to make Nunavik her first official destination once the government’s schedule is established.




She hopes to visit all 14 communities in Nunavik if logistics allow, although she acknowledged that it may require several trips.




“I will be present,” she said.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Man injured after shooting in Pangnirtung, deputy mayor says
content:
Pangnirtung is in shock after a shooting Tuesday afternoon injured a man, says deputy Mayor Markus Wilcke.




Wilcke said he heard shots Tuesday at around 4 p.m. and that the RCMP has since made an arrest.




“A lot of people were impacted, many of them children,” the deputy mayor said in an interview. “Pretty well everybody was impacted, directly or indirectly.”




He said the shots came from near the harbour. The suspect then entered residential streets and the area near the hamlet office.




“The RCMP did a good job and everyone is safe now,” Wilcke said.




Nunatsiaq News asked the RCMP about the incident but was told information about it would be available Thursday.




Wilcke says the hamlet will update the community through public statements and that counselling services will be available.
















He also said the community can expect a public meeting within the next few days to discuss what actions are needed to respond and prevent similar incidents in the future.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Boil water advisory issued for Taloyoak
content:
Nunavut’s Health Department issued a boil water advisory for Taloyoak due to the mechanical failure of a pump at the water treatment plant.




Any water used for consumption must be brought to a rolling boil for a minimum of one minute, either on the stove or with a kettle that does not have an automatic shut off, according to the advisory.




The advisory applies to water for drinking, preparing infant formulas, making juice or ice cubes, washing produce, cooking and brushing teeth.




Residents are also reminded that a camp stove should be used outdoors to avoid the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.




The Health Department will notify community members when the boil advisory has been lifted.

title: Nunavut duo wins at Pan-Arctic Vision
content:
A duo from Nunavut earned one of three honours at the fourth-annual Pan-Arctic Vision competition in Denmark on Oct. 2.




Christine Piunguałaq Tootoo

 of Rankin Inlet and 

Tooma Laisa

 of Iqaluit shared the award for “most feeling of community and togetherness.” 




The event, billed as the Arctic’s answer to the Eurovision Song Contest, took place at the Nordic House in Tórshavn, Faroe Islands.




“I love experiencing new cultures and languages,” Tootoo said in a preprepared video broadcast before her performance alongside Laisa. “Travelling gives me a zest for life.”




Travel was the theme of their traditional drum song, 

Kiviuq

.




Kiviuq is the name of a 

legendary Inuk

 who travelled across “the imaginary borders” of Inuit Nunangat, Tootoo said as she introduced the song from the stage.




Laisa softly drummed and hummed beside Tootoo, who recorded and looped Laisa’s voice. Then they sang their rendition of the legend.
















When the performance ended, the audience broke the silence with a roar of applause.




Icelandic rock band Falinn gjóður won “most revolutionary song” and Nuunu, a Greenlandic singer-songwriter who goes by one name, won “most Arctic song.”

title: Ottawa gives $77M to Arctic Bay for small craft harbour
content:
The federal government has announced $77-million in funding for a multi-use small craft harbour to be built in Arctic Bay.




The harbour will include a breakwater, launch ramp, fixed wharf for larger vessels, floating wharves for small craft vessels, dredging for the harbour basin and an entrance channel, according to a Fisheries and Oceans Canada press release issued on Oct. 2.




“This harbour will create opportunities for hunters, fishers and families to be more independent. Food sovereignty and economic prosperity will follow,” said Nunavut MP Lori Idlout in the release.




Construction began in August and will continue until 2029. It’s expected to be operational for the following open water season.




Pilitak Enterprises Ltd., an Inuit-owned construction company based in Iqaluit, is the contractor.




The contract created between the company and the hamlet includes an Inuit benefits plan to support local training and employment.




According to the release, the federal government is continuing to work with northern communities to help with development and create more resources for residents of the north such as this new harbour.

title: Baffinland seeks court approval for sale of assets
content:
Baffinland Iron Mines Corp. is seeking court approval to solicit bids on its shares and assets, which may include its Mary River Mine.




The company operates the mine on north Baffin Island and touts its ore as some of the highest-grade in the world. It began operations in 2014.




Baffinland 

sought creditor protection

The company

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Cambridge Bay helps keep Northwest Passage expedition moving
content:
A handful of bolts and a little help from Cambridge Bay residents kept a Polish sailing crew from being stranded in the Canadian Arctic.




Captains Alicja Latoń and Andrzej Górajek, who work for the Polish cruise and expedition company Natango, arrived in Cambridge Bay on Sept. 12 with a damaged propulsion system and were stuck for about a week.







Alicja Latoń, left, and Andrzej Górajek, right, crew members of the Polish sailing yacht Ocean A, stand ashore in Erebus Bay on Sept. 21, during the yacht’s eastbound return through the Canadian Northwest Passage. (Photo by Andrzej Górajek)




“It became the place that determined whether the entire second half of the expedition would be possible at all,” Górajek said in an email to Nunatsiaq News.




The pair is attempting to complete a trip that began July 29 with seven crew members. Their goal is to sail the Canadian section of the Northwest Passage in a single navigation season, from Upernavik, Greenland, to Tuktoyaktuk and back to Maniitsoq, Greenland.




“We wanted to find out whether a small sailing yacht could make the passage in both directions without wintering in between,” said Górajek, who is completing the return trip with Latoń.




The crew is calling the expedition, on the 75-foot Ocean A yacht, the “first known and documented” voyage rather than the first-ever, because historical records may be incomplete.

author: Corey Larocque
title: PQ’s Sonia Caron takes Ungava as her party wins minority government
content:
Nunavimmiut will be represented by Parti Québécois candidate Sonia Caron, who was elected Monday in Quebec’s geographically largest riding.




The PQ won a minority government in Monday’s provincial election, taking the largest number of seats in Quebec’s national assembly.




In Ungava, the massive riding that includes Nunavik and other parts of northern Quebec, Caron got 3,312 votes — 39.5 per cent of ballots cast, according to Élections Québec’s website.




Caron, originally from Chibougamau, is the director of professional development at the Centre de services scolaire de la Baie-James, which oversees trades programs in northern Quebec. She described herself in an 

interview

 last week as a lifelong supporter of the PQ.




She had a 25-year career in education before making the jump to politics this year after she was approached by several parties to be their candidate.




Caron told Nunatsiaq News she got into politics because the lack of front-line health services and the need for clean drinking water in many remote communities need urgent attention.




“I told myself, ‘We have to do something,’ because our region is undergoing major upheavals, and public services are constantly deteriorating,” Caron said in an interview before the election.

title: Quebec election day goes smoothly in Nunavik, officials say
content:
Officials say voting in the Ungava riding during Quebec’s provincial election is unfolding with no issues — a stark contrast from the 2025 federal election.




Polling stations are open in every community in the region, with two elections officers in each community, said Élections Québec spokesperson Julie St-Arnaud-Drolet in an email on Monday.




From Sept. 26 to Sept. 30, the advance polling dates in Nunavik, election staff helped residents get on the electors list to participate in the election, she said.




Election staff also recruited and trained locals to run the election, she added.




“In most communities, they were able to hire local residents; as a result, voters have access to services in Inuktitut today, on election day,” she said.




Kuujjuaq deputy Mayor Claude Gadbois said the voting process was smooth in his community.




“Everything seems to be under control,” Gadbois told Nunatsiaq News over Facebook on Monday afternoon.

Nunavimmiut were unable to cast ballots

title: Jason Iqaluq prepares to head to Iqaluit after byelection win
content:
Jason Iqaluq said Friday he was preparing to head to Iqaluit, after having been elected to represent Hudson Bay in Nunavut’s legislative assembly.




He said he found out the results of the byelection around 9 p.m. on Sept. 28, while relaxing at home and playing video games. Voting took place at the council chamber in Sanikiluaq, the sole community represented under the Hudson Bay riding.




“I was trying to keep my mind busy,” he said in a phone interview Friday, adding it was a pleasant surprise to find out he won.




Iqaluq has lived in Sanikiluaq his entire life. He’ll now commit himself full-time to politics, after working as a team leader at the airport and serving on the board of his local Arctic Co-op.




The trip from Sanikiluaq to Iqaluit was expected to be a long one, Iqaluq said, since he had to first fly from the island community in Hudson Bay to Winnipeg and stay overnight before he could catch a flight to Iqaluit on Sunday.




“I’m a bit anxious, but overall, I’m feeling that I can do this,” he said about the journey ahead.




He said his MLA orientation should begin this week and that he expects to be sworn in formally at the legislative assembly by the end of October.

On August 13, 1877, an unusual expedition left New London, Conn., bound for Cumberland Sound on the southeastern coast of Baffin Island. Known officially as the Howgate Preliminary Arctic Expedition, it was to be the first stage of a much grander enterprise planned by Captain Henry W. Howgate of the United States Army.




Howgate had been inspired by the recent British expedition to the High Arctic led by George Nares. With two ships, Nares had tried to reach the North Pole by way of Smith Sound, the narrow channel separating Ellesmere Island from Greenland. One ship, the Alert, had reached a point on Ellesmere Island farther north than any other ship had ever gone and wintered there.




Howgate thought that Americans should do one better than the British. He wanted to establish a permanent scientific colony at Lady Franklin Bay. For that, he would need Inuit — for he knew that none lived that far north — and dogs and skin clothing.




And so a plan was hatched that a preliminary expedition would travel to Cumberland Sound and winter there. It would be under the command of Captain George Tyson, a whaler well known to the Inuit of the sound. title: Education must continue to be the counter to denialism
content:
Education remains the best way to ensure Canadians understand the legacy of residential schools, to preserve the memories of children who died, and to care for survivors.




Earlier this week, after the Second Sons white nationalist group held an ominous demonstration just outside the Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc reserve near Kamloops, B.C., it became easier to understand the calls to criminalize residential school denialism.




A recurring theme at the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation ceremony on Parliament Hill, residential school denialism is becoming an alarming, disturbing phenomenon.




“We must … confront all forms of denialism that persist despite extensive historical records and an indisputable body of evidence, including first-hand survivor testimony,” Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour said during Wednesday’s event. “This leaves no room for doubt about the history and impact of the residential schools.”

title: Nunavut sports hall of fame inductions begin
content:
The Nunavut Sport Federation will induct its hall of fame’s inaugural class this weekend at the Aqsarniit hotel in Iqaluit.




The ceremony will take place during the Sport and Recreation Awards gala, where the Government of Nunavut recognizes the territory’s athletes, administrators, volunteers and coaches, according to a news release issued Friday by the Recreation and Parks Association of Nunavut.




Former NHL player Jordin Tootoo and Inuit games athlete Attima Hadlari are the first inductees into the hall.




Doors open to the gala at 6:30 p.m. The ceremony begins at 7 p.m.




From 2003 to 2017, Tootoo, played 723 games for the Nashville Predators, Detroit Red Wings, New Jersey Devils and Chicago Blackhawks. He racked up 65 goals, 96 assists and 1,010 penalty minutes during that time.




Hadlari was an Arctic sports athlete from Cambridge Bay who mastered the sealskin whip and went on to coach and officiate for young athletes participating in traditional Inuit games.




He also served in the first Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit Katimajiit, which gives expertise in how to apply Inuit traditional knowledge in government, from 2003 to 2005.
















Each year, the Nunavut Sports and Recreation Hall of Fame plans to take nominations from community members for inductees.

author: Randi Beers
title: The people we carry with us
content:
Annie Qimirpik




There are some people you expect to see forever. You see them around town, talk to them, tease each other, make plans without thinking too much about whether those plans will happen.




Because why wouldn’t they? When you live in a small community, people become part of the landscape of your life. You know where they live; that is their family. You recognize their voice before you see them.




And then suddenly they’re not there anymore.




I think one of the strangest things about grief is how ordinary the world continues to feel.




The sun is still rising. People still go to work. Kids still play outside. Planes come and go.




Life doesn’t stop just because someone you love is no longer living it with you.
















That can feel unfair, confusing and sometimes angering.




In a small community, loss is rarely experienced alone. When some dies, their absence can be part of the community itself.




There’s an empty place where they used to sit.




A name that comes up in conversation, a story someone tells, a song that suddenly means something: g

rief has a strange way of making ordinary things significant.




Sometimes, we talk so much about how someone died that we forget how they lived.




We remember tragedy because it’s the moment that changed everything. But the person was so more than the way we lost them. They were someone’s friend

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Quebec Conservative Marc Damant says Nunavik needs a local MNA
content:
Nunatsiaq News reached out to each candidate running in the Ungava riding ahead of Quebec’s Oct. 5 provincial election. Here’s what Quebec Conservative party candidate Marc Damant had to share with us.




Marc Damant says he wants to represent Ungava because Nunavik needs a local representative in the Quebec national assembly.




“I think it’s time that Nunavik had someone who was more of a full-time MNA,” said Damant, who lives in Kuujjuaq and is the Quebec Conservative party’s candidate in the Oct. 5 provincial election.




He said that previous MNAs didn’t enough of an interest in the region, and that people feel like they don’t matter.




While he acknowledged logistical and financial challenges make it difficult for candidates to visit Nunavik’s villages, he said nothing beats face-to-face conversation with electors.




“We have to do better for everyone,” said Damant, adding he’s the only candidate with posters up in Kuujjuaq right now.




Damant works as an airport manager for the Kativik Regional Government, where he’s responsible for airport operations and safety for multiple communities across Nunavik. From 2007 to 2014, he was a grounds operations co-ordinator for Air Inuit, a role that allowed him to travel across Nunavik.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Nunavik beneficiaries to see a 25% gas subsidy increase
content:
The Kativik Regional Government and Makivvik increased the gasoline subsidy for Inuit beneficiaries nearly 25 per cent Thursday.




The subsidy went to $1 per litre from 78 cents, following an a 32-cent jump in gasoline prices, according to a joint press release issued Wednesday.




“Gasoline in Nunavik is not a luxury. It is what allows people to get out on the land, harvest food, visit family and move within their communities,” Makivvik president Pita Aatami said in the release.




The subsidy is available for James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement beneficiaries.




Before the price and subsidy increases, beneficiaries were paying $1.69 per litre of gas. Now they will pay $1.78.




This subsidy is part of a wider suite of “cost-of-living” subsidies, to which the provincial government recently promised $155 million over the next six years, according to the release.




The other five subsidies impact food, airfare, harvesting equipment, elder assistance and household appliances.

title: I’m growing older than my anaanatsiaq will ever be
content:
Not everyone has the privilege of growing up with their grandparents presence and knowledge. It’s a blessing I didn’t have.




My anaanatsiaq was Tookasie Akpaleeapik. When my family, who is from Pond Inlet, was chosen to help the Inujjuarmiut (families from Inukjuak) adjust during the High Arctic Relocation in the 1950s, she followed to Grise Fiord.




Author Larry Audlaluk mentions my grandmother in his memoir 

What I Remember, What I Know: The Life of a High Arctic Exile

.




“When we arrived in Grise, after the aircraft’s engines stopped and the pilot opened the door to let us out, none of us wanted to be the first to get out. We were too shy. Tookashie was the brave one, getting out first.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Orange Shirt Day moves indoors in rainy Iqaluit
content:
Hundreds of Iqalummiut gathered inside the cadet hall for the sixth annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. It was a testament to the resolve of Indigenous Peoples who Canada’s residential school system tried to separate from their culture, language and traditions.




“We are still here,” said Gloria Uluqsi, the president of Nunavut Tunngavik Inc., the territory’s Inuit rights-holding organization.




Uluqsi seemed to hold back tears as she spoke from the podium, alternating between Inuktitut and English.




“We have endured so much,” she said. “Our families experienced hurt and loss. Inuit were separated from their families, their language, their culture and their way of life.”




Also known as Orange Shirt Day, the event remembers the experience of the estimated 150,000 Inuit, First Nations, and Métis children who attended 139 residential schools across Canada from the 1880s until as late as the 1990s.




“There’s elders, there’s youngsters — everybody from all walks of life,” said Eva Michael, communication specialist for event host Qikiqtani Inuit Association, as she observed more than 250 people pour into the building shortly after noon.

ᑭᓕᒃᕙᒃ ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐃᓚᐅᓂᐊᓯᔪᖅ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ




“ᐱᒃᑯᓇᑦᑎᐊᕐᑐᖅ,” ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 17-ᒥ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᓚᐅᖅᑎᓐᓇᒍ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᑐᙵᕕᒃᑯᓐᓂ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓄ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᒥᓂᔅᑕᓄ ᑐᒡᓕᕆᔭᐅᔪᓄᑦ, ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐃᓅᓯᖃᑦᑎᐊᕐᓂᕐᒥᓐ, ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᔪᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐃᒻᒥᓃᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᓂ.




ᑕᐃᑲᓂᓕ ᐃᑲᔪᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᒃᓴᖅᑖᕋᓱᖕᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᐊᖅᑯᓴᕆᐊᖅ ᒪᒥᓴᕐᕕᒃᒧᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂᑦ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ, ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖅ ᒪᓕᒃᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔪᓂᒃ ᓱᓕᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯ ᐊᑐᖁᓯᒪᔭᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐱᐅᓯᕚᓪᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᒪᒥᓴᖅᐸᓪᓕᐅᔾᔪᑎᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ.




“ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᖃᕐᓂᓐᓂ ᑕᑯᓯᒪᕗᖓ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᖃᓄᐃᙱᓐᓂᕐᓴᐅᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᑦᑎᐊᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᒪᐅᓇ ᐊᑐᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᒃᑯ  ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᔪᓂ,” ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.
















ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᖅᑕᐃᓕᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕐᓂᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᐅᓯᕚᓪᓕᒃᑲᓐᓂᕆᐊᖃᕐᒪᓐ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. ᐅᓄᕐᓂᕐᓴᐃᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᑖᒃᑯᓇᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᕐᓴᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᒪᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᖅᓴᕐᕕᒃᓴᓂ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᕐᓗᓂ, ᑖᓐᓇᑦᑕᐅᖅ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




“ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᒃᓴᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᑲᐅᑎᒋᔪᓐᓇᔾᔮᙱᑦᑐᑦ, ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᒃᑰᖓᓂᖓᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒥᒃ, ᐅᓇ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᑐᐃᓐᓇᐅᙱᑦᑐᖅ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᔫᓴᕝ ᒨᑖᒃ-ᕙᓚᐅᕙᔅ, ᐃᓚᐅᓕᕐᓂ ᐱᒋᐊᓕᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔩᑦ ᒫᔅᓯ 2025-ᒥ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᑉᓘᓇᒎ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᑦᑎᐊᕐᓇᕐᒪᓐ ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᕐᓂᑰᓪᓗᓂ ᐅᖃᐅᔾᔪᐃᔨᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᓕᒪᓂᕐᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᒻᒥᓃᖅᑎᑦᑎᑦᑕᐃᓕᓂᕐᒥᒃ.




“ᐱᓇᓱᑦᑎᐊᒻᒪᕆᖕᒪᓐ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᔭᕆᐊᓕᖕᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒧᑦ. ᐊᒃᑐᐃᓯᒪᓂᖃᕐᒪᓐ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᑯᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᑕᒪᑐᒧᖓ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᒨᑖᒃ-ᕙᓚᐅᕙᔅ.




ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔩᑦ ᐱᑕᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᑲᓇᑕ ᒪᓕᒃᑲᓗᐊᕐᒪᖔᑦ

title: Joy and remembrance on National Day for Truth and Reconciliation schedule
content:
Joy and celebration are on the schedule for many of the events throughout Inuit Nunangat for the sixth annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday.

title: Jason Iqaluq wins Hudson Bay byelection
content:
Jason Iqaluq will be the new MLA for the Hudson Bay constituency in Nunavut’s legislative assembly after winning Monday’s byelection over Nukaja Sala.




Iqaluq received 168 of the 228 ballots cast, while Sala received 54, according to Elections Nunavut’s website. Voter t

urnout was 48.61 per cent, with 228 of the 469 eligible voters casting ballots.




Voting took place Sept. 28 at the council chamber in Sanikiluaq. Advance voting was available from Sept. 14 to 24 at the hamlet office, and a mobile poll was held Sept. 21.




Iqaluq has lived in Sanikiluaq, the sole community in the Hudson Bay riding, his entire life. He works as a station team leader at the community’s airport and has served on the board of the local Arctic Co-op for about nine years.




The Hudson Bay seat became vacant after former MLA Daniel Qavvik resigned June 1. He was elected in 2022.

title: New airport terminal opens in Rankin Inlet
content:
Community members and politicians gathered at the Rankin Inlet airport Monday morning to celebrate the opening of its new terminal.




The event featured a qulliq lighting, prayer, ribbon-cutting and a barbecue, wrote Department of Transportation and Infrastructure spokesperson Greg Belanger in a public service announcement.




“The new larger air terminal building is a key transportation hub for the community of Rankin Inlet and the Kivalliq region, connecting people, goods and communities across Nunavut and the rest of Canada,” he wrote.




Transportation Minister George Hickes, Rankin Inlet South MLA Annie Tattuinee, Nunavut MP Lori Idlout, and Northern and Arctic Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand attended the ceremony.




Nunatsiaq News requested an interview with Hickes, but he was unavailable.




Chartrand was set to make a funding announcement on behalf of federal Transportation Minister Steven MacKinnon, according to the release.




Belanger did not respond to questions about the announcement.

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqaluit bylaw investigation ongoing 1 month after dog attack
content:
A dog attack that led to an 11-year-old girl being medevaced to Ottawa for surgery is still under investigation by the City of Iqaluit more than a month after the incident.




“The city does not have an update or findings to share at this time, and I can’t provide a date for when they will be available,” city spokesperson Geoff Byrne said in an email on Sept. 24, one month after Mia Joy Nowdlak-Fraser was mauled by a dog tethered in a backyard near a downtown playground.




Bylaw officers were not available to explain their investigation methodology, Byrne added.




On Aug. 28, the owner surrendered the dog to the municipality. On Sept. 3, it was killed.




On Aug. 25, an RCMP officer approached Nowdlak and her daughter, but the family felt uncomfortable and declined to speak, Nowdlak said in an interview Friday. No bylaw officer or city official has ever approached the family, she said.




She said her daughter is doing “OK” and she continues to support her.

ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖓ ᔮᓐ-ᕗᕌᓐᔪᐊ (ᔨᐊᕝ) ᐴᓂᐄ ᑐᓴᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᕕᒃᑐᖅᓯᒪᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᓄᑦ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 15-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᕋᓛᑦ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓂᑯᓂ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᐅᑎᖏᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᑕᐅᔪᒪᓂᖏᑦᑎᒍᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐅᒃᐱᕈᓱᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᒃᑲᓐᓂᕋᓱᒡᓗᑎᒃ ᑭᒃᑯᓕᒫᓂ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᓐᓂ.




ᐅᑯᐊ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᑐᕕᓃᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᔪᕕᓂᕐᓄᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᔪᓚᐃ 2025-ᒥ ᐸᓖᓯᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᕕᒃᒥ ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᖓᓱᐃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᑐᖂᑎᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋ ᑕᒫᓂ ᑕᖅᑭᑦ 8 ᐃᓗᐊᓂ. ᑎᓴᒪᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ – 6-ᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕ ᐊᕐᓇᖅ – ᐃᓅᔪᓐᓃᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑕᐅᓂᖏᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᓕᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ.




ᒪᐃᒥ ᑕᑯᔭᐅᔪᓐᓇᕐᓯᑎᑕᐅᓂᑰᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐅᓇ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᓯᓂᖅ ᐃᓚᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ 35-ᓂ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᔪᓂᒃ. 21 ᑖᒃᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᕋᓛᓄᑦ, 8 ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᖅᑕᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᒪᓕᒋᐊᖃᕐᓂᖃᖅᑐᓂᒃ, ᑕᓪᓕᒪᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᖅᑕᐅᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᖅ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐅᕈᑎᒋᔭᐅᙱᖢᓂ.




ᐊᑕᐅᓯᖅ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐊᓯᔾᔩᖁᔨᓯᒪᓪᓗᓂ ᑯᐸᐃᒃᒥ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᒪᓕᒐᖓᓂ ᐅᑯᐊ ᐊᕕᒃᑐᖅᓯᒪᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᐅᔪᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᒃᑲᓐᓂᕈᓐᓇᕐᓯᓯᒪᓗᑎᒃ ᐸᓖᓯᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᒪᓕᒐᐅᓂᐊᖅᑐᓂᒃ. ᐊᓯᐊᓕ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓂᑯ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᖅᑖᕋᓱᒃᑐ ᐸᓖᓯᓕᕆᓂᑰᒍᑎᒃ ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᐊᑐᖁᔭᐅᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᖅᑖᕋᓱᓕᕈᑎᒃ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᐅᑎᖏᓐᓂ.




“ᒪᕐᕈᐃᓂ ᐊᔾᔨᒌᙱᑦᑐᓂ ᐊᑐᓕᖁᔨᙱᓐᓇᑦᑕ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᓐᓂ. ᐃᓄᖕᓂ ᐸᓖᓯᖃᕈᒪᒐᑦᑕ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᑖᕆᔭᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂ ᐱᖃᑦᑕᕐᒥᓗᑎᒃ, ᐱᓇᓱᐊᒐᖏᑦ ᐊᔾᔨᒌᒡᓗᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᖏᑦ ᐊᔾᔨᒌᒡᓗᑎᒃ,” ᐴᓂᐄ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᓄᑦ ᐊᕕᒃᑐᖅᓯᒪᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᐃᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᑎᓪᓗᒋ ᐃᓄᒃᔪᐊᒃᒥᑦ.

content:
There was a lot of talk about listening in Rankin Inlet this week.




Naalagit — or Listen, in English — was the theme of the Kivalliq Trade Show.




It was impressive to see how closely the speakers embraced that simple theme in their speeches.




Political and business leaders such as Sen. Nancy Karetak-Lindell, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. president Gloria Uluqsi, Kivalliq Inuit Association president Koonoo Tattuinee, and Agnico Eagle Meliadine Mine general manager Marc-Olivier Vachon all tailored their speeches to include what it means to listen.




Karetak-Lindell told delegates Wednesday that listening to communities, youth and businesses can give us all a better understanding of their goals and aspirations. Communication must go both ways — speaking and listening — to make conversations productive and to lead to action, she said.

title: My travels as a small-town Inuk woman
content:
Annie Qimirpik




For someone from Kimmirut, a community of roughly 450 people, travelling out of town means getting on a plane, just like everywhere else in Nunavut.




There are no roads connecting us to the rest of the territory, let alone the rest of Canada. If you want to go somewhere else, you leave by air.




I grew up surrounded by vast landscape and in a very small population where everybody knows everybody. Often, everybody knows everybody’s business. There’s comfort in that kind of familiarity but there are also limitations. The world can feel far away.




This summer, over the course of six weeks, I travelled from six places: Iqaluit, Ottawa, Toronto, London, U.K., Clyde River and Cancun, Mexico.




Each was different and they gave me another way of looking at home. 




Iqaluit was the beginning. Although I’m from Kimmirut, Iqaluit has become familiar to me the way other places haven’t. It’s still Nunavut. You see people you know, still hear Inuktitut. Still surrounded by Arctic landscape.

Then there’s Ottawa: my first home away from home outside of Kimmirut. Moving there was my first real experience of being away from my community and having to figure things out for myself. What happened in 1999 which may have led us to this situation?

title: Ungava advance polls to open Saturday
content:
Advance polls for the Ungava riding in Quebec’s provincial election open Saturday, and staff from the provincial elections authority will be in each Nunavik community to help make voting more accessible.




Élections Québec spokesperson Julie St-Arnaud-Drolet said visiting remote communities ahead of the Oct. 5 election day is part of an effort to address the historically low voter turn out in Nunavik. It’s also a priority because they often struggle to contact electors through traditional means like the mail, she said.




“Last election, electors in Inuit communities didn’t receive their reminder cards, for example,” St-Arnaud-Drolet said about the 2022 election, in which they weren’t able to reach some residents because they didn’t have access to their post office box addresses.

title: Ubluriak Society offers free breakfast and lunch in Sanikiluaq
content:
A non-profit is offering free breakfast and lunch to hungry Sanikiluaq residents every weekday after the 

Ubluriak Society relaunched its 

food programs Monday.




“Free food twice a day — Monday to Friday,” said Isaac Mensah, the society’s operations manager, Wednesday in a phone interview.




Up to 70 people attend each meal, held at the Ubluriak Centre, which occupies the former hamlet building, he said.




The menus are simple, but filling.




Bacon and eggs, cereals and toast, and coffee are on hand for breakfast, while lunches include burgers and hot dogs, which two new full-time staff cook on portable grills. Two new full-time servers supervise the mealtimes.




On Wednesday, the society received by air from Winnipeg skids of frozen food that fill two freezers. The dry goods arrived from Montreal by sealift last month.




The society supplements its stock with other food purchased locally.

Food Banks Canada, a national charitable organization that supports food security initiatives, chipped in another $18,000.

title: Iqaluit resident starts fundraiser to support John Amagoalik’s care in Nunavut
content:
An online fundraiser is collecting money for the medical needs of John Amagoalik, revered by many as the “Father of Nunavut.”




Amagoalik, 78, had been residing at the Embassy West long-term care home in Ottawa after a surgery forced the partial amputation of one of his legs. He was lonely there, he has said, and eager to return to the territory he helped create through decades of land claim negotiations.




He returned

running out

“John Amagoalik dedicated more than 25 years of his life to creating Nunavut,” Hale wrote on her GoFundMe page.




The fundraiser, which had raised $2,600 as of Thursday morning, was created on Sept. 18.




Amagoalik has 

filed a civil suit

title: Deputy mayor warns against accuracy of former mayor’s AI-based website
content:

Smith cautioned against trusting Bell’s City Hall Record website during Tuesday’s council meeting and again in a social media post Wednesday morning.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Coast Guard officer wins ITK award for Inuit excellence
content:
Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami is celebrating an Inuk leader with the Canadian Coast Guard by giving them its Award for Inuit Excellence.




ITK President Natan Obed presented the award to Ciera Avinga Lee-Kooneeliusie during the national Inuit organization’s annual general meeting Sept. 10 in Kuujjuaq.




She will receive a $2,500 cash prize as well as tickets to attend ITK’s annual Tapiriit gala next year in Ottawa.




Lee-Kooneeliusie serves as a senior search and rescue program officer with the Coast Guard. She also holds a position as one of the Arctic Region’s lead first aid instructors, ensuring first aid training includes Inuit knowledge.




Raised in Pangnirtung, Lee-Kooneeliusie is the first Inuk woman to hold a leadership position within the Coast Guard’s Inshore Rescue Boat Program in Nunavut, said a Sept. 10 news release from ITK about the award.




She is known for supporting opportunities for Inuit within the Canadian Coast Guards programming that highlight recruitment, mentorship and training, the release said.




The ITK Awards have been presented annually for more than 20 years. This year’s Award for Inuit Excellence received 41 nominations.
















Last year’s recipient was Diana Neill-Anawak, for providing culturally responsive speech-language therapy.

title: Nunavut community organization receives $5.5M grant
content:
A non-profit in Nunavut has received a $5.5-million grant from the philanthropic arm of a mining company.




The money will go toward Annauma Community Foundation’s consensus granting program, which funds community-led initiatives across the territory, said a joint news release from Annauma spokesperson Lisa Milosavljevic and BHP Foundation spokesperson Nayomi Alexander.




BHP Foundation is a non-profit funded by BHP, an international mining company that specializes in iron ore, copper and metallurgical coal.




To date, Annauma’s program has awarded $4.3 million.




“This investment will benefit not only Annauma, but also Nunavut’s non-profit and charitable sector for years to come,” said Annauma co-founder Udlu Hanson in the release.




The grant will also support the Pirujaq Fund, which contributes to Annauma’s “long-term sustainability,” according to the release.




The Annauma Community Foundation focuses on “support for greater self-determination for Indigenous Peoples and preparing underrepresented young people for the future through education,” the release said.

title: Iqaluit council rejects renaming sewage lagoon ‘Trump Lake’
content:
A call to rename Iqaluit’s sewage lagoon Trump Lake died without a vote after no one seconded deputy Mayor Kim Smith’s motion during Tuesday night’s council meeting.




“I figure if (U.S. President Donald Trump) can rename landmarks, then so can we — and we can share a very polite Canadian giggle while we do,” Smith said as she presented her motion, adding no sign would be erected nor any public funds used if the lagoon were to be “symbolically renamed.”




Trump has signed executive orders to rename two bodies of water — the Gulf of Mexico in February 2025 and Lake Ontario in August. The new names, Gulf of America and Lake America respectively, are officially changed in the U.S. government’s Geographic Names Information System, and all federal departments and agencies must follow suit. 

But the change does not apply outside the United States.

The U.S. president has repeatedly mused, joked and threatened to make Canada the “51st state,” and his aggressive use of tariffs has caused economic uncertainty across the nation.

title: NTI president extols the power of an ‘informed Inuk’ at Kivalliq Trade Show
content:
The world is changing fast, as are interests in the North. There’s pressure to mine Nunavut’s natural resources and to develop infrastructure projects that support Arctic security and sovereignty.




That’s why Inuit need to listen to each other, to their communities and to their youth, says Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. president Gloria Uluqsi.




Big decisions lie ahead about the impacts of future economic activity.




“An informed Inuk is much harder to leave out of a decision that affects them,” Uluqsi said Tuesday in a speech to the Kivalliq Trade Show in Rankin Inlet this week.




She didn’t mention any projects by name. But there has been talk at the trade show about Agnico Eagle Mines’ gold mining and exploration, as well as the four nation-building projects going through the federal government’s Major Projects Office.




Those projects are the Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Project, the Grays Bay Road and Port Project, a hydroelectricity generator near Iqaluit, and a deepsea port in Qikiqtarjuaq.




Uluqsi leaned into the trade show’s theme — Naalagit, or “Listen” in English. She spoke about what it means to listen and what it means to be heard.

content:
Minor league softball is coming to Iqaluit in summer 2027, thanks to more than $220,000 raised by the Iqaluit Charity Golf Tournament in Gatineau, Que.




“This support will give more young people a chance to be active, learn new skills and take part in organized recreation,” said Iqaluit Mayor Solomon Awa Monday in a news release.




Organized by Outcrop Communications, more than 130 golfers took part in the Sept. 17 event, which also attracted approximately 30 corporate sponsors.




The donations are destined for the Ikajuqtiit Community Association, a non profit, Iqaluit-based organization that enhances recreational opportunities for local youth, including improvements to the Iqaluit ball diamond.




The funds will cover uniforms and equipment for the new league, said association chair Tom Fitzgerald Tuesday in a phone interview. 

The money will also pay for the installation of artificial turf in the outfield.

title: GN ready to airlift fuel to Igloolik if needed after shipment delayed 9 days
content:
The Government of Nunavut is on hand to fly diesel up to Igloolik, but officials don’t expect it will be needed.




The hamlet’s annual resupply of fuel was initially expected to arrive Sept. 17. That shipment has been 

delayed

 by nine days and now is expected to arrive Saturday.




Igloolik relies on diesel fuel for generating electricity, home heating and for the trucks that provide drinking water and sewage services. With reserves dwindling, the hamlet had asked residents to conserve water, and put the water trucks on a reduced schedule.




John Ivey, Igloolik’s senior administrative officer, said the hamlet has since lifted these restrictions after the territory assured him that the community wouldn’t be left without fuel.




The territory’s Petroleum Products Division is prepared to airlift fuel to the community if necessary, said Greg Belanger, a spokesperson for Transportation and Infrastructure Nunavut.




“The [petroleum products division] is closely monitoring inventory, and while we do not currently anticipate the need to airlift fuel, the option is available if required,” Belanger said.




The hamlet had approximately 80,000 litres of diesel fuel in its tanks as of Sept. 18, he said, an amount that should be “sufficient until resupply.”
















The department did not explain why the Igloolik’s fuel shipment was delayed.

content:
An Inuit cultural organization in Nunavik is criticizing Quebec’s decision to conduct its Oct. 5 provincial election entirely in French.




On Sept.1, Élections Québec announced that election information documents, which include the guide and reminder card that will be mailed to voters, would be French-only.




The move abides with Quebec’s language law, which 

became more strict

“Yesterday, I went to go get some mail and all I saw was French. I have no idea what it’s saying,” said William Tagoona, president of Avataq Cultural Institute.




His organization says Inuit voters will be disenfranchised if they have to navigate the provincial election in a language they don’t understand.




According to data collected in Nunavk in 2021, 8,770 out of 13,985 Indigenous respondents, or 62 per cent, reported they speak English only. A total of 1,550 respondents, or 11 per cent, reported they don’t speak English or French.




Tagoona said the decision is particularly troubling because Inuit have an exemption from certain Quebec language laws under the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement, signed in 1975.

title: Former Iqaluit mayor launches AI-driven site to monitor municipal issues
content:
How many new homes can Iqaluit’s water reservoir support?




Former Iqaluit mayor Kenny Bell is using artificial intelligence program ChatGPT to investigate this question and more, on his newly launched City Hall Record website.




The idea, Bell said, is to track long-term municipal issues that may have fallen by the wayside.




“I’m engaging as a citizen that’s also interested in our community,” Bell said Friday in a phone interview. “It’s really hard to go on the city website and find minutes and listen to records and stuff — especially if you don’t know what you’re looking for.”




Bell was elected to a four-year term as Iqaluit mayor in 2019. He 

resigned

 in 2022.

major issue

mandatory water conservation efforts

content:
Turns out, people in Iqaluit love to take a polar dip for a good cause.




About 90 people gathered at Apex beach Sept. 17 to jump into icy Frobisher Bay to raise awareness for suicide prevention.




The high was approximately 5 C.




For one week every September, Isaksimagit Inuusirmi Katujjiqatigiit Embrace Life Council hosts free events focused on healing, connection, resilience and suicide prevention to recognize Embrace Life Week.




This year’s programming started Sept. 10, to mark World Suicide Prevention Day, and ended for the first time with a polar dip, a change from the organization’s usual walk.




The idea was inspired by a polar dip event in Montreal for suicide prevention that Cpl. JP DuPont, a member of the Nunavut RCMP First Nations and Inuit Policing Program attended a couple years ago, said Tooma Laisa, spokesperson for Nunavut’s Embrace Life Council.

ᓂᕆᐅᒋᔭᐅᕗᖅ ᑐᓂᓯᓂᐊᕐᓂᖓᓂ 20 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᑲᑉᐱᕼᐃᓕᖅᑑᑉ ᐆᒻᒪᖅᑯᑎᖏᓐᓂ ᐱᔭᕆᐊᓕᖏᓐᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᓄᕌᕐᔪᐊᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒥᒃᖠᒋᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᓗᓂ ᐅᔭᕋᖕᓂᐊᕐᕕᐅᑉ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᑕᒫᒥ ᐅᖅᓱᐊᓗᑐᐃᓐᓇᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ 7 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒧᑦ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒡᓂᑯ ᐄᒍᓪᑯᓐᓂ.

author: Mosha Folger
title: Nunavut RCMP encouraged to continue wearing name tags
content:
While on-duty RCMP officers are no longer required to wear name tags on their uniforms nationally, Nunavut RCMP are going in a different direction.




Officers are encouraged to continue wearing name tags, with their names in English and Inuktitut syllabics as well, said an unsigned statement provided to Nunatsiaq News from the Nunavut RCMP.




The email lists three Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit principles as the Nunavut RCMP’s foundation: Inuuqatigiittiarniq, which means respecting others; tunnganarniq, or fostering a welcoming spirit; and aajiiqatigiingniq, which is reaching consensus through discussion.




The RCMP made the country-wide change to make name tags option on March 30, according to reports from the Globe and Mail.




Britt Bancroft, board director with the National Police Federation, the union that represents members and reservists with the RCMP, said the change was in response to officers being doxxed and having their families identified and harassed.




“We’re supportive of the option to remove name tags and instead display their badge for accountability when members feel a situation is unsafe,” Bancroft said in a statement to Nunatsiaq News.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Five candidates run for Ungava riding in Quebec election
content:
Five candidates are running in Quebec’s largest riding by land mass, which includes Nunavik, in the Oct. 5 provincial election.




Ungava MNA Denis Lamothe, who has held that seat since 2018, announced in January he would not seek re-election. His Coalition Avenir Québec party has nominated Amélie Béchard instead.




Originally from Matagami, she is a forestry engineer who specializes in operations management and forest planning. She has served on several boards of directors including the Matagami Commercial Development Corp.




The Parti Québécois nominated Sonia Caron, who manages the Baie-James Vocational Training Centre in Chibougamau.




In a statement posted on the party’s website, Caron said she hopes to give more decision-making power to northern communities, protect Indigenous Peoples’ ways of life, and ensure communities benefit from the North’s resources.




“I will be proud to be the first woman elected Member of the National Assembly for Ungava, and the first Indigenous person to represent this voice,” she said.




Antoine Côté will represent Québec Solidaire.
















Côté ran for councillor in Montreal in the 2025 municipal election. Parti Solitaire’s website does not yet list a biography or campaign priorities for Côté but says the information will be added.

ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᒃᒥ

 ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᑐᙵᓱᕝᕕᖓᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦᑯᓐᓄᑦ, ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐅᕋᓱᒐᑎ ᒪᓂᒻᒪᐃᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔾᔪᑎᒃᓴᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓇᓱᖕᓂᕐᒥᑦ.

author: Randi Beers
title: A case for rent control in Nunavut
content:
As temperatures drop and we start to prepare for another fall, we’re reminded of one of Nunavut’s most urgent problems: housing.




Andrew Morrison




We don’t need another study to make us aware of the crisis. We see it every day not only on the streets of Iqaluit, but in other, more hidden ways: students coming home with nowhere to live, families crammed into relatives’ homes and long-time Iqalummiut losing their staff housing when they retire. Too many people face various forms of homelessness in their own homeland.




The numbers back this up. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. reports that Iqaluit’s rental vacancy rate was just 0.3 per cent in 2025 — six empty units out of nearly 2,000. That leaves tenants with almost no alternatives and lets rents climb far beyond what many can afford.




Nunavut should freeze rents.




Rent control won’t solve the whole housing crisis. It won’t build the homes we badly need, and it won’t house everyone who is currently without shelter. But a rent freeze will help address staggering rental rates that seem to be going up every time we blink. 




Rent control won’t lower today’s already high rates, but it would limit how fast they can rise in future. Right now, Nunavut’s Residential Tenancies Act allows landlords to raise rent once every 12 months, with three months’ written notice — but sets no limit on the size of the increase.

title: Igloolik close to running out of fuel
content:
Igloolik is close to running out of fuel after an annual delivery didn’t arrive on time.




John Ivey, the hamlet’s senior administrative officer, said the Government of Nunavut told him the shipment that was expected to arrive Sept. 17 will now come on Sept. 26.




“It’s delayed for some reason,” he said in an interview.




Igloolik relies on diesel fuel for generating electricity to heat homes and for the trucks that provide drinking water and sewage services.




He said the hamlet is encouraging residents to conserve water and to limit electricity use.




“We got some assurance from the GN that they won’t let the town run out of fuel,” he said. “If it gets to the point where it’s getting pretty close, there could possibly be an airlift of fuel brought in, but we’re not at that stage.”




The hamlet has also contacted Nunavut’s emergency measures organization and local rangers, he said, who are prepared to help out if the shipment doesn’t arrive in time.
















He said technicians with the GN’s petroleum products division are in the community monitoring the situation and providing guidance. 




 “We’re pretty confident that they’re doing a good job keeping an eye on things,” Ivey said.




While the situation is serious, he said people don’t need to panic. 




“Unnecessary chatter on Facebook doesn’t really help the situation,” he said.

author: Daron Letts
title: ‘Listen up,’ say Kivalliq Trade Show organizers
content:
The Kivalliq Trade Show hasn’t started yet and it’s already breaking records.




With 60 exhibitors and more than 240 delegates, next week’s event is the biggest to date, says Kivalliq Trade Show Society president Robert Connelly.




“And our delegate numbers will keep going up as the event nears,” he said in a phone interview on Thursday.




With ongoing discussions about Arctic sovereignty, resource extraction and developing northern infrastructure, 

organizers are emphasizing the need to bring Inuit to the table, Connelly said.




“There has to be a lot of listening to make sure that the people of Nunavut and particularly Inuit are strongly engaged,” he said.




That idea is reflected in this year’s theme: Naalagit, the Inuktitut word for “listen.”




The panel discussions were built with that theme in mind. The first is called “Listening to Communities,” the second “Listening to Business” and the third “Listening to Youth.”
















Panelists across the three discussions include Christine Tootoo, vice-president of Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami’s National Inuit Youth Council; CBC journalist Juanita Taylor; historian Ryan Shackleton; and Albert Netser, with Arctic Fresh Projects.




Canada’s Arctic Ambassador Virginia Mearns is scheduled to give the keynote address on Tuesday morning, with other speakers such as Nunavut Senator Nancy Karetak-Lindell and Nunavut Tunng

author: Daron Letts
title: Arctic Talent: Dance like no one is listening
content:
John Manzo is Galaxy Cat, a multifarious artist who performs with panache.




He hosts the soundscape that animates the 200 guests who turn out to his twice-annual silent discos at Iqaluit’s Franco-Centre.




The fifth one is slated for Sept. 26. 




A silent disco involves three DJs spinning clashing genres of music that are pumped into participants’ headphones through radio frequencies. Each reveller tunes in to the channel of their choice.




Most come costumed. 




Fairies, astronauts, dinosaurs, fuzzy animals, pirates, space cowgirls, and at least one Cookie Monster have turned out to Galaxy Cat’s four past events.




Those without costumes don neon, fishnets, or just loud colours with unique hats or wigs.
















”Whatever makes you feel happy,” Manzo said.




The next event features DJ Miel who spins Latin music and house — a type of electronic music that speeds up to 130 beats per minute.




Beside her is DJ Will, whose musical taste is confined to the last two decades of the 20th century and the first decade of this one. 




Then there’s Galaxy Cat, who purrs for drum and bass — a 

sub-genre of electronic dance music with fast breakbeat drum patterns and heavy basslines.




“Because nobody else plays it in town,” Manzo said of why he chooses this style over others.




The opening hour belongs to Deadbeatz, who plays a mix of Afrobeats and disco.
